facts.claim: Most studies did not support the hypothesized associations of active and passive social media use with well-being.
facts.quote: Most studies did not support the hypothesized associations of ASMU and PSMU with well-/ill-being.

facts.claim: Passive Facebook usage causes declines in affective well-being over time by increasing envy.
facts.quote: It also demonstrated how passive Facebook usage leads to declines in affective well-being: by increasing envy.

facts.claim: Active social media use is linked to greater online support (r = .34), wellbeing (r = .15), positive affect (r = .11), and symptoms of anxiety (r = .12).
facts.quote: Most ESs were negligible (|r| < .10), with the exception of between-person associations for active SMU and greater online support (r = .34), wellbeing (r = .15), positive affect (r = .11), and symptoms of anxiety (r = .12)

facts.claim: Taking a break from Facebook causes life satisfaction to increase and emotions to become more positive, especially for passive Facebook users.
facts.quote: it was demonstrated that taking a break from Facebook has positive effects on the two dimensions of well-being: our life satisfaction increases and our emotions become more positive. Furthermore, it was demonstrated that these effects were significantly greater for heavy Facebook users, passive Facebook users, and users who tend to envy others on Facebook.

facts.claim: Passive social media use is linked to greater online support (r = .15).
facts.quote: and passive SMU and greater online support (r = .15).

facts.claim: Social media comparison (r=−0.30) and problematic social media use (r=−0.13) are linked to lower positive well-being.
facts.quote: Conversely, social media comparison (r=−0. 30) and problematic social media use (r=−0. 13) showed negative correlations with positive well-being.

research.angle: While passive Facebook use specifically causes declines in well-being through envy, many broader studies find mixed or negligible associations between active and passive use and mental health.
research.verdict: The evidence shows that passive use can specifically harm well-being via envy, but the overall relationship between social media types and mental health is inconsistent across different research methods.
research.caveat: Many studies found that the amount of time spent on social media may be too coarse a metric to lead to meaningful associations with well-being.
